title: The Slavic Cosmology (the three-layered world)
summary: The Slavic cosmos is three-layered: the Sky (Nebo) above, the Earth (Zemlya) in the middle, and the Underworld (Nav/Cherd) below. A world-axis (the world-tree, the 'axis mundi') connects the three layers. The Sky is the realm of Nebo and Perun; the Earth is the realm of the human world and the earth-gods; the Underworld is the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd) and Veles [S4][S5][S6].
uncertainty_notes: The three-layered cosmology is a scholarly reconstruction from folk belief and comparative evidence; it is not described in a single pre-Christian source [S6].

chapters.heading: The Sky (Nebo)
chapters.body: The highest heaven, the realm of Nebo and Perun [S4][S5].

chapters.heading: The Earth (Zemlya)
chapters.body: The human world, the realm of the earth-gods [S4][S5].

chapters.heading: The Underworld (Nav/Cherd)
chapters.body: The realm of the dead, the domain of Veles and Cherd [S4][S5][S6].

chapters.heading: The World-Axis
chapters.body: The world-tree (the 'axis mundi') connects the three layers [S5][S6].

title: The Perun-Veles Conflict (reconstructed)
summary: In the reconstructed 'Perun-Veles' conflict, the sky-thunder-god Perun and the underworld-serpent-god Veles are in opposition. This is a scholarly reconstruction (Ivanov & Toporov) of an Indo-European 'sky-father vs. underworld-serpent' duality, not a single attested Slavic myth [S6]. The 'conflict' is expressed in folk belief as the opposition of the thunder (Perun) and the serpent (Veles) [S5][S6].
uncertainty_notes: This is a scholarly reconstruction (Ivanov & Toporov), NOT a single attested Slavic myth. We present it explicitly as a reconstruction [S6].

chapters.heading: The Opposition
chapters.body: The thunder (Perun) vs. the serpent (Veles) — the reconstructed duality [S5][S6].

title: The Seasonal Cycle (Jarilo vs. Morana, reconstructed)
summary: In the reconstructed seasonal cycle, Jarilo (spring/youth) and Morana (winter/death) are in opposition. The cycle is expressed in folk ritual: the 'drowning of Marzanna' (the winter-goddess) in spring, and the 'Kupala' night (the midsummer fire-and-water festival) in the height of summer [S5][S6]. The 'spring kills winter, summer peaks, winter returns' is the reconstructed annual cycle [S5][S6].
uncertainty_notes: The seasonal cycle is reconstructed from well-attested folk rituals (the 'drowning of Marzanna', the 'Kupala' night); the 'myth' itself is a scholarly interpretation of these rituals [S6].

chapters.heading: Winter (Morana)
chapters.body: Morana, the winter/death goddess, rules the cold season [S5].

chapters.heading: The Drowning of Marzanna
chapters.body: In spring, an effigy of the winter-goddess is drowned to 'kill' winter [S5].

chapters.heading: The Kupala Night
chapters.body: At midsummer, the 'Kupala' fire-and-water festival (Jarilo's peak) [S5].

title: The Kupala Night (the midsummer fire-and-water festival)
summary: The 'Kupala' night (the midsummer solstice, around June 23/24) is a well-attested folk fire-and-water festival across Slavic lands: bonfires are lit, people leap over the fire, the 'Kupala' flower (the fern-flower) is sought, and the water is blessed [S5]. The 'Kupala' is associated with Jarilo (the spring/youth/sun god), though the relationship is debated [S5][S6].
uncertainty_notes: The 'Kupala' is a well-attested folk festival; its relationship to Jarilo (the sun/spring god) is debated [S5][S6].

chapters.heading: The Bonfires
chapters.body: Great bonfires are lit on the Kupala night [S5].

chapters.heading: Leaping the Fire
chapters.body: People leap over the fire (a rite of purification) [S5].

chapters.heading: The Fern-Flower
chapters.body: The 'Kupala' flower (the fern-flower) is sought (a rare, magical bloom) [S5].

chapters.heading: The Water
chapters.body: The water is blessed; the 'Kupala' water is collected [S5].

title: The Destruction of the Idols at Kiev (980 CE)
summary: In 980 CE, the pagan ruler Vladimir of Kiev (later baptized as Vladimir) ordered the destruction of the pagan idols. The great wooden idol of Perun (with a golden head and beard) was dragged from its hill by the Dnieper, beaten, and thrown into the river [S1][S3]. This is the oldest attested event in the Slavic pantheon's history — the moment of the Christianization of Kiev [S1][S3]. The 'Tale of the Destruction of the Idols' (a later retelling) describes the event in detail [S3].
uncertainty_notes: The Primary Chronicle (c. 1113 CE) is the oldest source but is a later literary retelling of 10th c. events; the 'Tale of the Destruction of the Idols' (16th-18th c.) is a much later retelling [S1][S3].

chapters.heading: The Pagan Kiev
chapters.body: The pagan idols stand on the hill by the Dnieper; Perun is the head [S1].

chapters.heading: Vladimir's Decision
chapters.body: Vladimir (influenced by the 'ambassador' episode) chooses Christianity [S1].

chapters.heading: The Destruction
chapters.body: The idols are dragged into the river; Perun is beaten and drowned [S1][S3].

chapters.heading: The Christianization
chapters.body: Kiev is baptized; the pagan pantheon is destroyed [S1].
